## 1. What you'll build, and why

Every type checker you have written so far decides each node the moment it reaches it. That works
because its rules are **local**: `+` looks at two operand types and answers, `check_expr` is handed
an expected type and pushes it down. Concept 05 called this bidirectional checking, and it got you
through five more concepts.

Overloading breaks it. Swift lets two functions share a name as long as their signatures differ —
and the *return type* counts as part of the signature:

```swift
func g() -> Int    { return 1 }
func g() -> Double { return 2.5 }
let c: Double = g()
let d: Int    = g()
```

That is a real Swift program; `swiftc` compiles it and it prints `2.5` then `1`. Two identical call
sites, two different functions. Nothing about `g()` decides which one is meant — only the type the
context wants back does, and `infer` has nothing to look at when it gets there.

There is no order in which a local rule could reach the answer. The fix is not a better rule; it is
a different architecture, and it is the one swiftc actually uses.

- **You implement:** `unify` and `simplify` (the part that needs no guessing), `solve` (the search
  over overload choices, with scopes, scoring and a budget), and `csapply` (writing the answer back
  onto the tree). Plus, when you want it, the **splitter** — an optional second rung that is the
  difference between a compiler and a toy.
- **Outcome:** your compiler resolves overloads on the parameter type, on the arity, and on the
  return type alone, and the programs **run and match `swiftc` byte for byte**.
- **Prereqs:** 05 (bidirectional checking, literal defaulting), 07 (functions, two-pass collection
  of signatures), 09 (SIL and LLVM, which this concept carries so the programs can run).

**A leaf.** This concept forks concept 09's pipeline rather than extending concept 40's, so the
solver is the only new part and nothing downstream depends on it. Concept 14 did the same.

## 2. Concepts, in depth

### The wall

Trace `let d: Int = g()` through concept 05's machinery and watch it fail.

`check_stmt` sees an annotation, resolves `Int`, and calls `check_expr value TInt`. `check_expr`
has no arm for a call, so it falls through to `infer`, which reaches `Ast.Call ("g", [])` and looks
`g` up. In concept 07 that lookup returned one signature. Now it returns two, and `infer` must
return a type. It can pick the first, or the last, or report an ambiguity — every one of those is
wrong for some program, and the information that would settle it (`Int`, four tokens to the left)
was thrown away one call earlier when `check_expr` gave up and delegated.

You could patch it: give `check_expr` a `Call` arm that filters the overload set by the expected
type. That handles this example. It does not handle `let d: Int = f(g())`, where the argument's
overload and the result's overload constrain each other, and neither is known first. Each patch
buys one program.

The problem is the *shape*: a checker that must produce an answer at every node can only use the
information that reached that node. Overload resolution needs information from elsewhere in the
expression, and sometimes from outside it.

### Generate, solve, apply

So stop producing answers. Walk the tree once and write down what must be **true**, in a language
with a word for "I do not know yet". Then solve the whole system at once. Then walk the tree again
and write the answers onto it.

@fig-solve follows the program above through all three.

![One program through the three passes: `csgen` writes the system down, `cssolver` searches it, `csapply` writes the answer onto the tree. Swap `Int` for `Double` in the annotation and the same call site resolves to the other declaration.](figs/solve.png){#fig-solve}

Three files, and they are swiftc's three files:

| ours | swiftc | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `csgen.ml` | `lib/Sema/CSGen.cpp` | one walk; allocates a type variable per expression, emits constraints, decides nothing |
| `cssolver.ml` | `lib/Sema/CSSolver.cpp`, `CSStep.cpp` | finds an assignment of the variables that satisfies every constraint |
| `csapply.ml` | `lib/Sema/CSApply.cpp` | one walk; puts the types and the chosen declarations onto the tree |

The split is not tidiness. Generation cannot fail to be complete — it never has to choose, so there
is no wrong choice to make. Solving cannot look at the program — it only sees constraints, so it
cannot accidentally depend on the order the source was written in. And applying cannot re-derive
anything, because by then the answer exists. Each pass can only get its own job wrong.

### The language of facts

Three constraint kinds are enough for this subset. swiftc's `Constraint.h` has about forty, most of
them about conformance and subtyping.

```ocaml
type ty = Con of Types.ty      (* a type we know *)
        | Var of int           (* $T0 — one we do not *)

type t =
  | Equal       of ty * ty * span            (* these two are the same type *)
  | Literal     of ty * literal_kind * span  (* a literal of this kind may be this type *)
  | Disjunction of disjunction               (* EXACTLY ONE alternative holds *)
```

`Var` is the case concept 05's `Types.ty` did not have, and its absence is exactly why that checker
had to decide early. There was no way to write down "the answer is whatever it turns out to be".

**`Literal` replaces a tree walk.** Concept 05 modelled Swift's polymorphic literals with
`is_int_literal`, a predicate that walked an expression asking "could this whole subtree have been a
Double?". Here the same fact is one constraint on one variable:

```
$T0 : ExpressibleByIntegerLiteral
```

The walk disappears, and with it both of the quadratics §6 exercise 5 of concept 05 is about. The
solver never asks the question twice because the answer is written down the first time.

**`Disjunction` is the only one that cannot be solved by looking at it.** `Equal` is work for
`unify`; `Literal` is a membership test once its type is known. A disjunction has to be *searched*,
and that is where the exponent in "exponential in the worst case" comes from.

An overload set becomes one:

```
g is one of { (Int) -> Int    [ $T0 == Int    ]
            | (Double) -> Double [ $T0 == Double ] }
```

Run `--emit-constraints` on any program in this concept and you will see the real thing.

### The grammar does not change

This is the first concept in the course that adds **no syntax at all**. The lexer, the parser and
the AST are concept 07's, untouched. What changes is what a program is allowed to *mean*:

| before (07) | now (41) |
|---|---|
| a name identifies one function | a name identifies a **set**, and the signatures must differ |
| a second `func f` is `invalid redeclaration of 'f'` | only a second one with the **same signature** is |
| `Tast.Fn_call` carries a name | it carries a name **and the index of the declaration chosen** |

That last row is the concept's whole output. A name is no longer a unique identifier, which has a
consequence downstream — see *Two functions, one name, one symbol* below.

### Solving: what needs no guess, and what does

`simplify` runs the worklist and solves everything decidable:

- `Equal (a, b)` — hand it to `unify`. Resolve both sides first: what matters is what they are
  *now*, not what they were written as. Two concrete types must agree; a variable takes the other
  side.
- `Literal (t, kind)` — if `t` has resolved to a concrete type, check it is one the literal may
  take. If it has not, **keep the constraint**. The default is only applied when the search is
  over, and a constraint dropped here is a program wrongly accepted later.
- `Disjunction` — keep it. That is the search's job.

What `unify` does *not* need here is an occurs check. This subset has no type constructors — no
`Array<T>`, no `(A) -> B` as a first-class type — so there is no way to build a type that contains
a variable, and therefore no way to bind `$T0` to something containing `$T0`. Every Hindley–Milner
implementation needs one; ours is honestly vacuous, and saying so is better than pretending the
code is complete.

`solve` handles the rest: take a disjunction, try each alternative, keep what works.

### Scopes, and why a wrong guess is cheap

Trying an alternative makes bindings that may have to be undone. The mechanism is a **trail**: a
list of every variable bound, most recent first. A scope is a position in that list; leaving one
pops back to it, removing each binding on the way.

```ocaml
let entry = scope_of s in
(match solve search s (choice.implies @ rest) with ...);
restore s entry
```

Undoing costs exactly what the guess added — not a copy of the solution, not a rebuild. swiftc's is
`ConstraintSystem.h:1323`'s `SolverScope`, with a trail large enough to have its own header
(`CSTrail.h`) and its own budget. This is what lets the search afford to be exhaustive.

### Scoring, or why `1 + 2` is not Double arithmetic

`1 + 2` has more than one solution. Int arithmetic satisfies every constraint; so does Double, with
both literals taking their non-default type. Both are *correct* — the system does not distinguish
them, so something outside it must.

swiftc ranks solutions on about a dozen axes (`Sema/Score.h`). One of them is enough here, and it is
one of theirs:

```ocaml
(* SK_NonDefaultLiteral — Score.h:59 *)
let score s = (* one point for each integer literal that ended up a Double *)
```

Lowest score wins. `1 + 2` scores 0 as Ints and 2 as Doubles, so Ints win. `1 + 2.0` cannot be Ints
at all, so the Double solution wins by being the only one. The rule is small and it is doing real
work: delete it and take the first solution instead, and every literal in the language silently
becomes a Double.

This is also why the search explores **every** alternative rather than stopping at the first that
works. Answering yes-or-no needs one solution; answering *correctly* needs the best one.

### It is exponential, and swiftc says so

> Solving the constraint systems generated by the Swift language can, in the worst case, require
> exponential time. Even the classic Hindley-Milner type inference algorithm requires exponential
> time, and the Swift type system introduces additional complications, especially overload
> resolution.
>
> — `swift/docs/TypeChecker.md:552`

*n* disjunctions of *k* alternatives is *k^n* combinations. Propagation prunes hard — commit to
`Int` at one operator and every `Double` alternative below it dies immediately — but nothing
guarantees the pruning happens, and when the alternatives are independent nothing prunes at all.

So the search gets a hard budget and **reports** rather than hangs. Ours counts scopes; swiftc has
four ceilings (`LangOptions.h:959-969` — an expression timeout, 512 MB of memory, a million scopes,
64 MB of trail) and one diagnostic, which is the one everybody has seen:

```
error: the compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time;
       try breaking up the expression into distinct sub-expressions
```

Ours says exactly that. §5 shows how to provoke it.

### The splitter, which is not optional

Two constraints can only affect each other if they share a type variable, directly or through a
chain. Constraints that share none are independent problems, and solving them *together* multiplies
searches that could have been added: *k^(m+n)* where *k^m + k^n* would do.

swiftc splits the constraint graph into connected components and solves each alone
(`CSStep.h:232`'s `SplitterStep`; the constraint graph is the docs' first Performance heading). Our
`components` starts out returning `[ cs ]` — one group, everything together. That is *correct*, and
every test in this concept passes with it.

It is also the difference between a compiler and a toy, and §5 measures exactly how much.

### Diagnosing a failure, which is the hard part

A constraint solver starts at a disadvantage here, and it is worth being clear about why. Concept
05's checker knew which rule failed, because a rule had to fail for it to stop. A search that comes
back empty knows only that the system is unsatisfiable — not which constraint is to blame, because
it never committed to one, and not which operand is wrong, because it tried both ways.

swiftc recovers the blame by solving **again with "fixes" enabled**: a fix lets a failing constraint
succeed at a score penalty, so the search completes, and the fixes it had to apply *are* the
diagnosis. That machinery is `lib/Sema/CSDiagnostics.cpp`, and it is about nine thousand lines.

`Cssolver.diagnose` (given) is the crude version, in two stages:

1. **Is an overload set wrong on its own?** For each disjunction, test every alternative against
   the operand constraints only. If none survives, that operator or call is to blame, and it is
   reported with concept 05's wording. Note *operand constraints only*: testing against the whole
   system would blame `+` for `let x: Bool = 1 + 2`, and `+` really can add two Ints.
2. **Otherwise the conflict is with a type someone wrote.** Drop each written type in turn and
   solve what is left. If the rest of the program has an answer, that answer is what the annotation
   disagrees with — and naming both is swiftc's wording. Dropping a constraint to see what the
   others say is the same move as a fix, in the one case this subset needs.

Every message, against the oracle:

| program | ours | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `let b = 1 + true` | `binary operator '+' cannot be applied to operands of type 'Int' and 'Bool'` | words it as an argument conversion, because its `+` is generic |
| `let c = true < false` | `binary operator '<' cannot be applied to two 'Bool' operands` | **identical** |
| `let s = "a" + 1` | `binary operator '+' cannot be applied to operands of type 'String' and 'Int'` | **identical** |
| `let y: String = 1` | `cannot convert value of type 'Int' to specified type 'String'` | **identical** |
| `let x: Bool = 1 + 2` | `cannot convert value of type 'Int' to specified type 'Bool'` | suggests `!= 0`, which needs a fix-it we do not have |
| `f(1, 2)` with no 2-arity `f` | `no exact matches in call to global function 'f'` | **identical** |
| two identical `func f` | `invalid redeclaration of 'f'` | **identical** |

### Two functions, one name, one symbol

Overloading has a consequence that reaches past the checker, and this is the first place in the
course where it bites: **a name is no longer a unique identifier, and a symbol must be.** Three
functions called `show` cannot all be `@show` in the IR.

So SILGen mangles, using the index the solver recorded:

```
sil @show$0(%0 : $Int) -> $Int
sil @show$1(%0 : $Double) -> $Int
sil @show$2(%0 : $String) -> $Int
```

Swift does the same thing for the same reason, with a scheme that encodes the whole signature —
`show(_: Int) -> Int` becomes `$s4main4showyS2iF`. Run `swiftc -emit-assembly` on an overloaded
program and you can read them. The index is enough for us because the checker has already chosen;
what matters is that *something* distinguishes them, and that the checker is what decides.

### Honest limits

- **No type constructors**, so unification is union-find plus concrete equality, and the occurs
  check is vacuous. Real inference variables inside `Array<T>` or a function type would need it.
- **No generics.** swiftc's hardest disjunctions come from generic overloads with conformance
  requirements; ours come from a handful of concrete signatures.
- **One score axis.** `SK_NonDefaultLiteral` and nothing else, so two solutions that differ any
  other way tie, and a tie is reported as an ambiguity rather than ranked.
- **Diagnosis is two heuristics**, not a fix-based replay. §6 exercise 3 is the swiftc route.
- **Double printing** is concept 09's `%g`, so `3.0` prints as `3`. Inherited, documented there,
  and the reason no oracle program prints a Double.

## 3. Build it, step by step

Your concept 07 front end and concept 09 back end are filled in; you write the `TODO(41)` holes.
§4 lists which test file each one turns green.

| file | holes | what you write |
|---|---|---|
| `cssolver.ml` | 3 | `unify`, `simplify`, `solve` |
| `csapply.ml` | 1 | the expression walk that builds the `Tast` |
| `cssolver.ml` | *optional* | `components` — the splitter, `TODO(41e)` |

### The traps, one per hole

**`TODO(41a)` `unify`.** Resolve both sides before comparing: what matters is what they are now,
not what they were written as. Every binding you make must go on the **trail**, or a scope cannot
undo it — and a scope that cannot undo is a solver that gets one guess.

**`TODO(41b)` `simplify`.** The three kinds are not alike, and the `Literal` case is where this
goes wrong quietly. A literal constraint whose variable is still open must be **handed back**, not
dropped: `let s: String = 1` binds the variable through the annotation long after the literal
constraint went by, and if nothing keeps it, nothing ever looks again.

**`TODO(41c)` `solve`.** Simplify first. If no disjunction is left, you have a solution — but check
the literal constraints `simplify` handed back before you call it one, for the reason above. If a
disjunction is left, try each alternative in its own scope and **keep the best-scoring**, not the
first that works. And count scopes: raise `Too_complex` when the budget is gone, rather than
running until someone kills the compiler.

**`TODO(41d)` `csapply`.** One arm per `Ast.expr` constructor, each returning the matching `Tast`
form with the type `type_of` gives for its span. The arms are mechanical, which is the point. The
one that is not is `Call`: `Tast.Fn_call` wants the **index** of the declaration chosen, and
`g.Csgen.chosen` has it keyed by the call's span. Leave it out and the tree still says "a call to
something named `f`", which is the question this concept exists to answer.

**`TODO(41e)` the splitter.** Optional, and `[ cs ]` is correct. Union-find over the variables is
the shape: two constraints belong together when they mention one in common. Constraints that
mention none can go anywhere.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase9-inference/41-constraint-solver
```

| file | flag | green with | what it pins |
|---|---|---|---|
| `csgen.t` | `--emit-constraints` | *nothing* — generation is given | what a literal, an operator, and an overload set each turn into |
| `solver-units` (alcotest) | — | `41a`, then `41b` | `unify` on concrete types, chains, and the trail; `simplify` on each constraint kind |
| `solve.t` | `--emit-tast` | `41a-d` | the type on every node, and which declaration each call resolved to |
| `diagnostics.t` | `--typecheck` | `41a-d` | both stages of `diagnose`, and the wording of each |
| `run.t` | `build` | `41a-d` | what the programs **print** — the only thing that can tell `show#0` from `show#1` |
| `oracle.t` | `build` | everything | 10 programs compiled and run by both compilers, stdout compared byte for byte |

`csgen.t` passing on an untouched skeleton is not a bug: generation is given, and the file is there
to be read.

`run.t` and `oracle.t` are the point. Accept-or-reject cannot see overload resolution at all —
`show(1.5)` type-checks whichever `show` you pick. Three declarations that return `1`, `2` and `3`
turn the resolution into output, and then `swiftc` can be asked whether it agrees.

## 5. Benchmark it

The splitter, measured. Take *n* statements that share no type variable — each one an
independent two-way choice, because an integer literal could be either overload's argument:

```swift
func p(_ x: Int) -> Int { return x }
func p(_ x: Double) -> Int { return 0 }
print(p(0))
print(p(1))
…
```

With `components` returning `[ cs ]` the solver sees one system with *n* independent
disjunctions and walks 2^n combinations of them. Split into connected components it solves *n*
two-way choices, one at a time. Best of three, after a warm-up:

| n | one group | split |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0.003 s | 0.002 s |
| 12 | 0.005 s | 0.002 s |
| 13 | 0.007 s | 0.002 s |
| **14** | **budget exhausted** | 0.002 s |
| 20 | budget exhausted | 0.004 s |
| 40 | budget exhausted | 0.003 s |

Read the left column as doubling — which it is, until it hits the 20 000-scope ceiling at
2^14 ≈ 16 000 and stops. Fourteen one-line statements, nothing nested, nothing clever, and the
compiler answers:

```
error: the compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time;
       try breaking up the expression into distinct sub-expressions
```

The right column is flat to forty and would be flat to four hundred.

That is why the constraint graph is the first heading under *Performance* in swiftc's own design
document, and why "optional second rung" describes the code rather than the idea. It is also
worth knowing the shape of the failure: the message blames the *expression*, and the expression
is fine. What was too complex was solving it together with thirteen unrelated ones.

## 6. Exercises

1. **A second score axis.** Two solutions that differ only in something `SK_NonDefaultLiteral`
   cannot see currently tie, and a tie is an ambiguity. Add one of swiftc's others — favour a
   non-generic over a generic, or an exact match over a conversion — and find a program whose
   verdict changes.
2. **Favoured choices.** The search tries alternatives in declaration order. Try the one whose
   parameter types already match the operands' resolved types first, and count scopes explored
   before and after on the §5 benchmark.
3. **Diagnose with fixes.** Replace `diagnose`'s two heuristics with swiftc's method: re-solve
   allowing any single constraint to fail at a score penalty, and report the one that had to. This
   is the exercise that makes the error messages good rather than adequate.
4. **Occurs check.** Give the language one type constructor — an array type, say — so a variable
   can appear inside a type. Now `unify` can build a cycle, and needs the check every
   Hindley–Milner implementation has.
5. **Cache the solved components.** Two statements with the same constraint shape are solved twice.
   Key the component's solution by its shape and reuse it.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You replaced a bidirectional checker with the architecture swiftc uses: **generate** constraints
without deciding anything, **solve** them by search with scopes and a score, **apply** the answer to
the tree. The payoff is a thing local rules cannot express at all — a call resolved by the type its
context wants back — and the cost is a search that is exponential in the worst case, a budget to
stop it, and a diagnosis problem that is genuinely harder than the one you had before.

Three ideas from here are worth carrying:

- **Deciding late is a design, not a delay.** Every fact the generator writes down instead of acting
  on is a fact that can be combined with one discovered elsewhere.
- **The recorded decision is the output.** `Fn_call` carries an index, `Tast` carries types, SILGen
  mangles from both — the same claim concept 05 made about literals, now about declarations.
- **Search needs a budget and a story for failure.** Both are load-bearing, and both are where the
  real compiler spends its complexity.

This is a leaf: nothing downstream depends on it. Concepts 21–24 build generics on top of concept
07's simpler checker, and the honest reading of that is that the course teaches the constraint
solver here, where it can be seen whole, rather than threading it through nineteen concepts that do
not need it.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

Mirrors `solution/cssolver.ml` and `solution/csapply.ml`, minus their frozen headers. **Try
§3 first — this is the answer.** `make check-solution C=phase9-inference/41-constraint-solver`
builds and runs exactly this.

### `cssolver.ml`

```ocaml
(* --- the substitution (ConstraintSystem.h's type-variable bindings) ------------------- *)

type solution = {
  bindings : (int, Constraints.ty) Hashtbl.t;
  (* the variables bound so far, most recent first. A scope is a position in this list, so
     undoing a guess costs only what the guess added. swiftc calls it the trail, and
     gives it a whole header: swift/include/swift/Sema/CSTrail.h. *)
  mutable trail : int list;
  (* which variables a literal constraint applies to, and of which kind: needed to default
     anything still unbound when the search ends, and to score one solution against
     another *)
  literals : (int, Constraints.literal_kind) Hashtbl.t;
}

let empty () : solution =
  { bindings = Hashtbl.create 64; trail = []; literals = Hashtbl.create 64 }

let rec resolve (s : solution) (t : Constraints.ty) : Constraints.ty =
  match t with
  | Constraints.Con _ -> t
  | Constraints.Var n -> (
      match Hashtbl.find_opt s.bindings n with None -> t | Some t' -> resolve s t')

(* The types a literal of each kind may take, most preferred FIRST — the head is the
literal's
   DEFAULT type. Swift declares these in the standard library rather than the compiler:
   `public typealias IntegerLiteralType = Int` in stdlib/public/core/Policy.swift. *)
let literal_types = function
  | Constraints.Int_literal -> [ Types.TInt; Types.TDouble ]
  | Constraints.Double_literal -> [ Types.TDouble ]

(* --- scopes (ConstraintSystem.h:1323, `struct SolverScope`) ------------------------------
   Trying an overload makes bindings that may have to be undone. Remember where the trail
   was on entry; undo back to it on the way out. That is what makes a wrong guess cheap,
   and it is why the search can afford to be exhaustive. *)

type scope = int list

let scope_of (s : solution) : scope = s.trail

let restore (s : solution) (entry : scope) : unit =
  let rec undo () =
    if s.trail != entry then
      match s.trail with
      | [] -> ()
      | v :: rest ->
          Hashtbl.remove s.bindings v;
          s.trail <- rest;
          undo ()
  in
  undo ()

(* --- the budget (LangOptions.h:959-969) --------------------------------------------------
   The search is exponential in the worst case, so it gets a hard limit and REPORTS rather
   than hangs. swiftc has four of these — an expression timeout, a memory ceiling, a scope
   count and a trail size — and the diagnostic they raise is the one everyone has seen. *)

exception Too_complex

let scope_budget = 20_000

type search = { mutable scopes_explored : int }

(* --- TODO(41a): unify ----------------------------------------------------------------- *)
let unify (s : solution) (a : Constraints.ty) (b : Constraints.ty) : bool =
  match (resolve s a, resolve s b) with
  | Constraints.Con x, Constraints.Con y -> Types.equal x y
  | Constraints.Var n, other | other, Constraints.Var n -> (
      match other with
      | Constraints.Var m when m = n -> true (* already the same variable *)
      | _ ->
          Hashtbl.replace s.bindings n other;
          s.trail <- n :: s.trail;
          true)

(* --- TODO(41b): simplify -------------------------------------------------------------- *)
let rec simplify (s : solution) (cs : Constraints.t list) : Constraints.t list option =
  match cs with
  | [] -> Some []
  | Constraints.Equal (a, b, _) :: rest ->
      if unify s a b then simplify s rest else None
  | (Constraints.Literal (t, kind, _) as c) :: rest -> (
      match resolve s t with
      | Constraints.Var _ -> (
          (* still unknown — keep it; the default is applied when the search finishes *)
          match simplify s rest with None -> None | Some kept -> Some (c :: kept))
      | Constraints.Con concrete ->
          if List.exists (Types.equal concrete) (literal_types kind) then simplify s rest
          else None)
  | (Constraints.Disjunction _ as d) :: rest -> (
      (* a choice cannot be made by looking at it — hand it to the search *)
      match simplify s rest with None -> None | Some kept -> Some (d :: kept))

(* --- the score (Score.h, `SK_NonDefaultLiteral` at :59) ----------------------------------
   Several assignments can satisfy the same system, and the checker has to pick one. swiftc
   ranks them on a dozen axes; one is enough here, and it is one of theirs: a literal
   that had to leave its default type counts against a solution. That single rule is why
   `1 + 2` is Int arithmetic even though Double arithmetic satisfies every constraint
   just as well. *)
let score (s : solution) : int =
  Hashtbl.fold
    (fun n kind acc ->
      match (kind, resolve s (Constraints.Var n)) with
      | Constraints.Int_literal, Constraints.Con Types.TDouble -> acc + 1
      | _ -> acc)
    s.literals 0

(* --- TODO(41c): the search (CSStep.cpp's DisjunctionStep) ----------------------------- *)
let rec solve (search : search) (s : solution) (cs : Constraints.t list) :
    (solution * int) option =
  search.scopes_explored <- search.scopes_explored + 1;
  if search.scopes_explored > scope_budget then raise Too_complex;
  match simplify s cs with
  | None -> None
  | Some remaining -> (
      match
        List.partition (function Constraints.Disjunction _ -> true | _ -> false) remaining
      with
      | [], _ ->
          (* nothing left to choose, so this is a solution. A snapshot, because the caller
             will undo these bindings before trying the next alternative.

             DEFAULTS ARE NOT APPLIED HERE. A variable still unbound is one nothing has
             pinned, and `solve_system` gives it its default type once every component has
             had its say — doing it here would default variables belonging to components
             that have not been solved yet, and `let b: Double = f(1)` would be rejected
             because the literal was made an Int before the annotation was ever read. *)
          let final = { s with bindings = Hashtbl.copy s.bindings } in
          (* a literal constraint that was still open when it was met is KEPT, and this is
             where it is finally answered: `let s: String = 1` binds the variable to String
             through the annotation long after the literal constraint went by, and nothing
             would ever have looked at it again. *)
          let literals_hold =
            List.for_all
              (function
                | Constraints.Literal (t, kind, _) -> (
                    match resolve final t with
                    | Constraints.Con c -> List.exists (Types.equal c) (literal_types kind)
                    | Constraints.Var _ -> true)
                | _ -> true)
              remaining
          in
          if literals_hold then Some (final, score final) else None
      | Constraints.Disjunction d :: other_disjunctions, simple ->
          let rest = other_disjunctions @ simple in
          let best = ref None in
          List.iter
            (fun (c : Constraints.choice) ->
              let entry = scope_of s in
              (match solve search s (c.Constraints.implies @ rest) with
              | None -> ()
              | Some (candidate, candidate_score) -> (
                  (* keep the BEST, not the first: taking the first success would be enough
                     to answer yes or no, but the score is what makes `1 + 2` an Int *)
                  match !best with
                  | Some (_, best_score) when best_score <= candidate_score -> ()
                  | _ -> best := Some (candidate, candidate_score)));
              restore s entry)
            d.Constraints.choices;
          !best
      | _ :: _, _ -> None)

(* --- the splitter, TODO(41e) (CSStep.h:232, `SplitterStep`) ------------------------------
   The single most important thing the real solver does for performance, and the reason an
   ordinary Swift file compiles at all. Constraints that share no type variable cannot
   affect each other, so solving them together multiplies two searches that could have
   been added. Split the system into connected components of the constraint graph, solve
   each alone, and put the answers back together — k^(m+n) becomes k^m + k^n. *)

let rec vars_of (c : Constraints.t) : int list =
  let of_ty = function Constraints.Var n -> [ n ] | Constraints.Con _ -> [] in
  match c with
  | Constraints.Equal (a, b, _) -> of_ty a @ of_ty b
  | Constraints.Literal (a, _, _) -> of_ty a
  | Constraints.Disjunction d ->
      List.concat_map
        (fun (ch : Constraints.choice) -> List.concat_map vars_of ch.Constraints.implies)
        d.Constraints.choices

let components (cs : Constraints.t list) : Constraints.t list list =
  (* union-find over type variables; two constraints join a component when they mention a
     variable in common. This is swiftc's ConstraintGraph, in the form this subset needs. *)
  let parent = Hashtbl.create 64 in
  let rec find v =
    match Hashtbl.find_opt parent v with
    | None -> v
    | Some p when p = v -> v
    | Some p ->
        let r = find p in
        Hashtbl.replace parent v r;
        r
  in
  let union a b =
    let ra = find a and rb = find b in
    if ra <> rb then Hashtbl.replace parent ra rb
  in
  List.iter
    (fun c ->
      match vars_of c with
      | [] -> ()
      | v :: rest ->
          if not (Hashtbl.mem parent v) then Hashtbl.replace parent v v;
          List.iter
            (fun w ->
              if not (Hashtbl.mem parent w) then Hashtbl.replace parent w w;
              union v w)
            rest)
    cs;
  let buckets = Hashtbl.create 16 in
  let ungrouped = ref [] in
  List.iter
    (fun c ->
      match vars_of c with
      | [] -> ungrouped := c :: !ungrouped
      | v :: _ ->
          let r = find v in
          Hashtbl.replace buckets r (c :: Option.value ~default:[] (Hashtbl.find_opt
          buckets r)))
    cs;
  let grouped = Hashtbl.fold (fun _ v acc -> List.rev v :: acc) buckets [] in
  match !ungrouped with [] -> grouped | u -> List.rev u :: grouped

let solve_system (search : search) (s : solution) (cs : Constraints.t list) :
    (solution * int) option =
  let default_the_rest () =
    (* every literal nobody pinned takes its default type — `IntegerLiteralType = Int` *)
    Hashtbl.iter
      (fun n kind ->
        match resolve s (Constraints.Var n) with
        | Constraints.Var m ->
            Hashtbl.replace s.bindings m (Constraints.Con (List.hd (literal_types kind)))
        | Constraints.Con _ -> ())
      s.literals
  in
  let rec go acc_score = function
    | [] ->
        default_the_rest ();
        Some (s, acc_score)
    | component :: rest -> (
        match solve search s component with
        | None -> None
        | Some (part, part_score) ->
            (* components share no variables, so merging is a union — no conflict is
            possible *) Hashtbl.iter (fun k v -> Hashtbl.replace s.bindings k v)
            part.bindings; go (acc_score + part_score) rest)
  in
  go 0 (components cs)

(* --- diagnosing a FAILED search (given)
---------------------------------------------------
   The hard part of any constraint solver, and the reason swiftc has a directory for it
   (lib/Sema/CSDiagnostics.cpp, ~9000 lines). When the search comes back empty you know the
   system has no solution — and nothing else. Not which constraint is to blame, because the
   solver never committed to one; not which operand is wrong, because it tried both ways.

   swiftc recovers the blame by solving AGAIN with "fixes" enabled: a fix lets a failing
   constraint succeed at a score penalty, so the search completes, and the fixes it had to
   apply are the diagnosis. Here is the crude version — find the first overload set where no
   alternative survives on its own, and report it the way concept 05 would have, from the
   operand types the disjunction carries. §6 exercise 3 is the swiftc route. *)
let diagnose (search : search) (diagnostics : Diagnostics.sink) (s : solution)
    (cs : Constraints.t list) : bool =
  (* the literal constraints alone: what an operand can be, before anything outside asks *)
  let literal_only =
    List.filter (function Constraints.Literal _ -> true | _ -> false) cs
  in
  ignore (simplify s literal_only);
  let reported = ref false in
  List.iter
    (fun c ->
      match c with
      | Constraints.Disjunction d when not !reported ->
          let viable =
            List.exists
              (fun (ch : Constraints.choice) ->
                let entry = scope_of s in
                (* against the operand constraints, NOT the whole system. A disjunction is
                   only to blame if nothing it offers fits what its operands are — if the
                   conflict is with something further out, say an annotation, blaming the
                   operator says something false: `+` really can add two Ints. *)
                let ok = simplify s (ch.Constraints.implies @ literal_only) <> None in
                restore s entry;
                ok)
              d.Constraints.choices
          in
          if not viable then (
            reported := true;
            (* for the MESSAGE only, a variable still open is shown at its default type:
               the reader wrote `1`, and being told the operand is `_` helps nobody *)
            let shown =
              List.map
                (fun a ->
                  match resolve s a with
                  | Constraints.Con t -> Types.string_of_ty t
                  | Constraints.Var n -> (
                      match Hashtbl.find_opt s.literals n with
                      | Some kind -> Types.string_of_ty (List.hd (literal_types kind))
                      | None -> "_"))
                d.Constraints.args
            in
            Diagnostics.error diagnostics d.Constraints.dspan
              (match (d.Constraints.is_operator, shown) with
              (* concept 05's two operator wordings, and swiftc's, chosen the same way *)
              | true, [ a; b ] when a = b ->
                  Printf.sprintf
                    "binary operator '%s' cannot be applied to two '%s' operands"
                    d.Constraints.what a
              | true, [ a; b ] ->
                  Printf.sprintf
                    "binary operator '%s' cannot be applied to operands of type '%s' and \
                     '%s'"
                    d.Constraints.what a b
              | true, [ a ] ->
                  Printf.sprintf
                    "unary operator '%s' cannot be applied to an operand of type '%s'"
                    d.Constraints.what a
              (* a CALL is a different shape, and swiftc words it differently. Its `abs` and
                 `min` are generic rather than overloaded, so it reaches for the conformance
                 wording ("requires that 'String' conform to 'SignedNumeric'"); ours are an
                 overload set, and this is what swiftc says when a genuine overload set has
                 no match. The modelling difference is §2's, not a bug. *)
              | false, _ ->
                  Printf.sprintf "no exact matches in call to global function '%s'"
                    d.Constraints.what
              | true, _ ->
                  Printf.sprintf "operator '%s' cannot be applied to these operands"
                    d.Constraints.what))
      | _ -> ())
    cs;
  if !reported then true
  else
    (* Nothing offered by any overload set is wrong in itself, so the conflict comes from a
       type someone WROTE. Drop each written type in turn and solve what is left: if the
       rest of the program has an answer, that answer is what the annotation disagrees
       with, and naming both is swiftc's wording. Dropping a constraint to see what the
       others say is the same move as swiftc's "fixes", in the one case this subset
       needs. *)
    let written =
      List.filter
        (function Constraints.Equal (_, Constraints.Con _, _) -> true | _ -> false)
        cs
    in
    List.exists
      (fun c ->
        match c with
        | Constraints.Equal (a, Constraints.Con wanted, span) ->
            let others = List.filter (fun c' -> c' != c) cs in
            let probe = empty () in
            Hashtbl.iter (fun k v -> Hashtbl.replace probe.literals k v) s.literals;
            (match solve search probe others with
            | Some (sol, _) -> (
                match resolve sol a with
                | Constraints.Con got when not (Types.equal got wanted) ->
                    Diagnostics.error diagnostics span
                      (Printf.sprintf
                         "cannot convert value of type '%s' to specified type '%s'"
                         (Types.string_of_ty got) (Types.string_of_ty wanted));
                    true
                | _ -> false)
            | None -> false)
        | _ -> false)
      written

(* --- the entry point (given) ---------------------------------------------------------- *)

let span_of_program (program : Ast.program) : Token.span =
  match program.Ast.items with
  | Ast.IStmt (Ast.Let { span; _ }) :: _
  | Ast.IStmt (Ast.Assign { span; _ }) :: _
  | Ast.IStmt (Ast.Expr_stmt (_, span)) :: _ ->
      span
  | Ast.IFunc { fspan; _ } :: _ -> fspan
  | _ -> Token.dummy_span

let check (program : Ast.program) (diagnostics : Diagnostics.sink) : Tast.program option =
  let g = Csgen.create diagnostics in
  Csgen.generate_program g program;
  let s = empty () in
  List.iter
    (function
      | Constraints.Literal (Constraints.Var n, kind, _) -> Hashtbl.replace s.literals n
      kind
      | _ -> ())
    g.Csgen.constraints;
  let search = { scopes_explored = 0 } in
  let outcome =
    try solve_system search s g.Csgen.constraints
    with Too_complex ->
      Diagnostics.error diagnostics (span_of_program program)
        "the compiler is unable to type-check this expression in reasonable time; try \
         breaking up the expression into distinct sub-expressions";
      None
  in
  match outcome with
  | None ->
      if not (Diagnostics.has_errors diagnostics) then
        if
          not
            (let fresh_state = empty () in
             Hashtbl.iter (fun k v -> Hashtbl.replace fresh_state.literals k v) s.literals;
             diagnose { scopes_explored = 0 } diagnostics fresh_state g.Csgen.constraints)
        then
          (* no single overload set is to blame — the system is unsatisfiable as a whole,
             which is what swiftc means by this message *)
          Diagnostics.error diagnostics (span_of_program program)
            "type of expression is ambiguous without a type annotation";
      None
  | Some (sol, _) ->
      if Diagnostics.has_errors diagnostics then None
      else (
        (* record which alternative each disjunction settled on, so csapply can name it *)
        List.iter
          (function
            | Constraints.Disjunction d ->
                List.iter
                  (fun (ch : Constraints.choice) ->
                    if
                      List.for_all
                        (function
                          | Constraints.Equal (a, b, _) -> (
                              match (resolve sol a, resolve sol b) with
                              | Constraints.Con x, Constraints.Con y -> Types.equal x y
                              | _ -> false)
                          | _ -> true)
                        ch.Constraints.implies
                    then
                      if not (Hashtbl.mem g.Csgen.chosen d.Constraints.dspan) then
                        Hashtbl.replace g.Csgen.chosen d.Constraints.dspan
                          ch.Constraints.index)
                  d.Constraints.choices
            | _ -> ())
          g.Csgen.constraints;
        Some (Csapply.program g (Csapply.solution_of sol.bindings) program))
```

### `csapply.ml`

```ocaml
type solution = (int, Constraints.ty) Hashtbl.t

let solution_of (bindings : (int, Constraints.ty) Hashtbl.t) : solution = bindings

let rec resolve (s : solution) (t : Constraints.ty) : Constraints.ty =
  match t with
  | Constraints.Con _ -> t
  | Constraints.Var n -> (
      match Hashtbl.find_opt s n with None -> t | Some t' -> resolve s t')

(* The type the solver gave this node. A node with no entry never had a variable — it was
   concrete the moment it was generated. *)
let type_of (g : Csgen.t) (s : solution) (span : Token.span) : Types.ty =
  match Hashtbl.find_opt g.Csgen.types_of span with
  | None -> Types.TInt
  | Some t -> (
      match resolve s t with Constraints.Con c -> c | Constraints.Var _ -> Types.TInt)

let rec expr (g : Csgen.t) (s : solution) (expression : Ast.expr) : Tast.expr =
  let span = Ast.expr_span expression in
  let mk e = { Tast.e; ty = type_of g s span; span } in
  match expression with
  | Ast.Int_lit (n, _) -> mk (Tast.Int_lit n)
  | Ast.Double_lit (f, _) -> mk (Tast.Double_lit f)
  | Ast.Bool_lit (b, _) -> mk (Tast.Bool_lit b)
  | Ast.String_lit (str, _) -> mk (Tast.String_lit str)
  | Ast.Var (x, _) -> mk (Tast.Local x)
  | Ast.Unary (op, e0, _) -> mk (Tast.Unary (op, expr g s e0))
  | Ast.Binary (op, l, r, _) -> mk (Tast.Binary (op, expr g s l, expr g s r))
  | Ast.Ascribe (e0, _, _) -> mk (Tast.Coerce (expr g s e0))
  | Ast.Call ("print", [ a ], _) -> mk (Tast.Print (expr g s a))
  | Ast.Call ("print", _, _) -> mk (Tast.Print (mk (Tast.Int_lit 0)))
  | Ast.Call (f, args, _) ->
      (* the index the solver settled on. Without it the tree would still say "a call to
         something named f", which is exactly the question this concept exists to answer. *)
      let chosen = Option.value ~default:0 (Hashtbl.find_opt g.Csgen.chosen span) in
      mk (Tast.Fn_call (f, chosen, List.map (expr g s) args))

let rec stmt (g : Csgen.t) (s : solution) (st : Ast.stmt) : Tast.stmt =
  match st with
  | Ast.Let { name; is_var; value; span; _ } ->
      Tast.Let { name; is_var; value = expr g s value; span }
  | Ast.Assign { name; value; span } -> Tast.Assign { name; value = expr g s value; span }
  | Ast.Expr_stmt (e, _) -> Tast.Expr_stmt (expr g s e)
  | Ast.If { cond; then_blk; else_blk; span } ->
      Tast.If
        {
          cond = expr g s cond;
          then_blk = List.map (stmt g s) then_blk;
          else_blk = Option.map (List.map (stmt g s)) else_blk;
          span;
        }
  | Ast.While { cond; body; span } ->
      Tast.While { cond = expr g s cond; body = List.map (stmt g s) body; span }
  | Ast.For { var; lo; hi; body; span } ->
      Tast.For
        { var; lo = expr g s lo; hi = expr g s hi; body = List.map (stmt g s) body; span }
  | Ast.Break span -> Tast.Break span
  | Ast.Continue span -> Tast.Continue span
  | Ast.Return (v, span) -> Tast.Return (Option.map (expr g s) v, span)

let func (g : Csgen.t) (s : solution) (f : Ast.func_decl) : Tast.func_decl =
  let sg = Csgen.signature_of g f in
  {
    Tast.fname = f.Ast.fname;
    params =
      List.map2
        (fun (p : Ast.param) t -> { Tast.pname = p.Ast.pname; pty = t })
        f.Ast.params sg.Constraints.params;
    ret = sg.Constraints.result;
    body = List.map (stmt g s) f.Ast.body;
    fspan = f.Ast.fspan;
  }

let program (g : Csgen.t) (s : solution) (p : Ast.program) : Tast.program =
  {
    Tast.items =
      List.map
        (function
          | Ast.IFunc f -> Tast.IFunc (func g s f)
          | Ast.IStmt st -> Tast.IStmt (stmt g s st))
        p.Ast.items;
  }
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 4 — the occurs check

The one exercise with a short answer worth writing out, because the bug it prevents is silent.
With a type constructor in the language, `unify ($T0, Array($T0))` would bind `$T0` to a type that
contains `$T0`. Nothing detects it at binding time; `resolve` then loops forever the next time it
is asked. The guard is one walk, before the bind:

```ocaml
let rec occurs (s : solution) (n : int) (t : Constraints.ty) : bool =
  match resolve s t with
  | Constraints.Var m -> m = n
  | Constraints.Array inner -> occurs s n inner
  | Constraints.Con _ -> false
```

and `unify` refuses rather than binding when it holds. swiftc does the same check in
`ConstraintSystem::matchTypes`.
